title: No Signer is wired in the composition root; TenantKeyStore holds only the default algorithm
description:
asterius_domain::Signer has exactly one implementor, asterius_jose::LocalKeyStore, which is used only by tests. main.rs builds a TenantKeyStore and registers it as Arc<dyn KeyStore>; nothing in the binary can sign anything. The first grant handler (ast-a05.2) needs a Signer, so this blocks it.

Two things have to be decided together:

1. What implements Signer over PostgreSQL. crates/store-pg/src/keys.rs deliberately does not: 'Signing through it would mean unwrapping the private key on every token — for a cloud KMS, a network round trip per token. The composition root loads the active key once and signs from memory.' So something has to hold the unwrapped keys.

2. How many keys it holds. After ast-a05.12 a Signer must answer for any SigningAlgorithm a client registered, not just the tenant default — so 'the active key' is now 'the active key per algorithm'. TenantKeyStore::apply_schedule calls apply_schedule(SigningAlgorithm::DEFAULT) and active_signing_key(SigningAlgorithm::DEFAULT); both need to iterate SigningAlgorithm::ALL, or the deployment has to decide which algorithms it offers and refuse registrations for the others (ast-a05.13).

Also unresolved: a cached in-memory signer has to notice a rotation. A key promoted from pending to active by the background sweep must reach the signer, or it keeps signing with a retiring key until the process restarts.
acceptance_criteria: The binary holds an Arc<dyn Signer> that answers for every algorithm the tenant has an active key for, refreshes across a rotation, and returns DomainError::NoSigningKey for an algorithm it has no key for. A test issues a token through it for each algorithm in SigningAlgorithm::ALL.

title: Signer cannot be told which algorithm to sign with (wrong at_hash for ES256/PS256 clients)
description:
Signer::sign takes (tenant, typ, claims) and picks the tenant's active key, preferring EdDSA. An ID token must be signed with the *client's* registered id_token_signed_response_alg: OIDC Core §3.1.3.7 has the client check the algorithm, and §3.1.3.6 ties at_hash to it — the hash is derived from the signing algorithm, so signing with EdDSA while the client expects ES256 produces an at_hash the client computes differently and therefore rejects.

Concretely: a client that registers ES256 or PS256 today gets an ID token it cannot validate. This is a correctness bug, not a hardening item.

UnsignedToken::required_algorithm() already carries the constraint out of the token builder, and PgKeyRepository::active_signing_key(alg) already selects by algorithm — so the fix is either a Signer::sign_with(tenant, algorithm, typ, claims) on the port, or a direct call at the token endpoint that bypasses the convenience method. The port is shared domain surface, which is why the agent that found this did not change it.

Found by the ast-a05.4 agent, which built at_hash correctly and then noticed nothing could give it the right algorithm.
acceptance_criteria: A client registered for ES256 receives an ID token signed with ES256 and an at_hash computed with SHA-256; one registered for EdDSA gets EdDSA and SHA-512. A test registers a client for each algorithm in SigningAlgorithm::ALL and verifies the issued token against the registered algorithm.
notes: ADR-0003 pins EdDSA to Ed25519, which is what makes the at_hash pairing total: RFC 8037 §3.1 leaves the variant to the key subtype and RFC 8032 §5.1 makes Ed25519's hash SHA-512.
close_reason: Signer::sign now takes Option<SigningAlgorithm>; ID tokens are signed with the client's registered id_token_signed_response_alg and a tenant lacking the key is refused with DomainError::NoSigningKey. Commit 52f8f71 on worktree-agent-ad472e25831926ff9.

title: Interaction HTTP handlers and the PostgreSQL adapter
description: ast-2vk.1 landed the interaction engine — the id and its __Host- cookie, the CSRF token, the state machine, the templates and their escaping proofs. What is left is the wiring: GET/POST /interaction/{id}/{stage} handlers resuming through Interaction::resume (path id and cookie must both match) and rendering through Document; the store adapter against auth_requests keyed by interaction_id_hash; destroying the interaction and clearing the cookie on a browser mismatch; and the error page path with a correlation id logged beside the real reason.
acceptance_criteria: A request whose path id and cookie disagree gets the error page, the row is gone and the cookie is cleared. A POST without the issued CSRF token gets 403. Reloading a stage twice before deciding succeeds. An expired interaction is indistinguishable from an absent one to the browser.

close_reason: Handlers and adapter merged; 15 new tests; full gate green. Credential verification is the typed UserAuthentication seam, owned by ast-2vk.5.

title: Per-tenant pairwise salt has no storage (blocks minting any subject)
description:
ast-2vk.6 landed derive_subject() and PgUserRepository::subject(), but both take the pairwise salt as an *argument* — nothing persists it and the baseline schema has no column for it. Until that exists there is no production path that mints a subject at all, so this blocks every flow that issues an id_token.

The salt is key material: it must be sealed under the existing Kek port exactly as signing keys are (a *_ciphertext column, see crates/store-pg/src/key_store.rs and 0001_baseline.sql signing_keys), not stored in plaintext. A leaked salt lets an attacker correlate every pairwise sub across every sector for that tenant, which is the entire property pairwise subjects exist to provide.

Note the rotation constraint recorded in docs/threat-model.md: the salt can never be rotated, because every derived sub is already stored and OIDC Core §8 says a Subject Identifier is never reassigned. Recovering from a leak means reissuing every identifier — a relying-party migration. Generate it once, at tenant creation.
acceptance_criteria: Migration adds an encrypted per-tenant salt column sealed under Kek; a tenant gets a salt at creation; derive_subject reads it from the store rather than taking it as an argument; a DB test proves the raw column is ciphertext and that the same (user, sector) yields a stable sub across processes.
notes: Reported by the ast-2vk.6 agent as out of scope (it was told not to write migrations). Depends on ast-mxc.3's Kek wiring, which has landed.
close_reason: Per-tenant pairwise salt now has storage: tenant_pairwise_salts, sealed under the Kek port, written once at tenant creation. derive_subject is a method on PairwiseSalt and PgUserRepository::subject reads the salt from the store rather than taking it as an argument. Rotation refused by an UPDATE trigger and by the absence of any mutator.

title: Strict CSP (nonce + strict-dynamic) & security headers on every HTML response
description:
Middleware sets per-response nonce and headers: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'nonce-{n}' 'strict-dynamic'; style-src 'nonce-{n}'; img-src 'self' data:; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; form-action 'self' {redirect-origin-when-form_post}; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none'; object-src 'none'`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`, `Permissions-Policy: publickey-credentials-get=(self), publickey-credentials-create=(self)`, `Cache-Control: no-store` on interaction pages.

Spec: FAPI 2.0 SP §5.2.3 (browser endpoints: HSTS, no CORS on authorization endpoint); RFC 9700 §4 (clickjacking, referrer leakage); CSP Level 3; RFC 6797 (HSTS).

It says nothing about CSP. The normative source for this story is RFC 9700 §4.16 ('Authorization servers MUST prevent clickjacking attacks' ... 'SHOULD also use Content Security Policy (CSP) level 2 or greater') plus §4.2.4 for Referrer-Policy and the no-third-party-resources rule.

title: Refresh tokens: opaque, grant-bound, no rotation (FAPI 2.0), revocable
description:
Opaque ≥256-bit refresh tokens stored as SHA-256 digests with grant, client, scopes, absolute and idle expiry. No rotation by default; a time-boxed rotation mode exists only for migrations (FAPI Note 1) and offers the old token for retry within a grace window.

Spec: RFC 6749 §1.5, §6 (refresh request: grant_type=refresh_token, refresh_token, scope ⊆ original), §10.4; OIDC Core §12.1–12.3 (refresh: ID Token MAY be returned; `sub` MUST match; new nonce not required); FAPI 2.0 SP §5.3.2.1 item 9 ('shall not use refresh token rotation except in extraordinary circumstances'), Note 1, §6.1 (long-lived grants → short ATs + RTs); RFC 9449 §5 (refresh tokens for public clients bound to DPoP key; confidential clients: new AT bound to the proof key presented); RFC 9700 §4.14 (refresh token protection: sender-constrained or rotation — we use client authentication + optional key binding).

Depends on: E08_02, E07_03

- Refresh request requires client authentication and a DPoP proof; the new access token's `cnf.jkt` is the presented proof key; tenant option `bind_refresh_to_dpop_key` rejects a different key (`invalid_grant`).
- Requested `scope` ⊄ granted → `invalid_scope`; narrowing allowed; `openid` present → new ID token with same `sub` and `auth_time`.
- Same refresh token value returned unchanged (no rotation) by default; migration mode issues a new token and accepts the old one for `grace_seconds` (test both).

title: DPoP (RFC 9449): proof validation, jkt binding, nonce, `dpop_jkt` in PAR, metadata
description:
Proof validation middleware for token, PAR (dpop_jkt correlation), UserInfo, introspection (optional), grant-management, SSF-management and AuthZEN endpoints. Replay store in PostgreSQL keyed by (tenant, jkt, jti) with TTL = iat window.

Spec: RFC 9449 §4.1 (`DPoP` header), §4.2 (proof JWT: typ dpop+jwt, alg asymmetric ≠ none, jwk public key; claims jti, htm, htu, iat, nonce, ath), §4.3 (checking: exactly one header; parse; typ; alg; signature with jwk; jti replay; htm/htu match; iat window; nonce), §5 (token request: `token_type: DPoP`; error `invalid_dpop_proof`), §6.1 (`cnf.jkt` = JWK thumbprint RFC 7638), §8 (AS-provided nonce: `use_dpop_nonce` 400 + `DPoP-Nonce` header), §10.1 (`dpop_jkt` authorization request parameter), §10.2 (in PAR), §11 (`dpop_signing_alg_values_supported`), §12 (`dpop_bound_access_tokens`), §13 (security: htu normalisation, replay); FAPI 2.0 SP §5.3.2.1 items 4–5 (sender-constrained via DPoP), 10 (nonce MAY), 12 (must support code binding to DPoP key), 13 (skew).

Depends on: E02_04, E08_01, E02_06

Definition of done (project rule): spec-derived or conformance-suite test passes; fuzz target exists for every new parser/validator; threat-model note updated; no new `unsafe`; generated crypto/parsing code is not done until a human has read the cited spec sections.
acceptance_criteria:
- Two `DPoP` headers → `invalid_dpop_proof`/`invalid_request`; missing `typ`/wrong `typ`, `alg` outside {ES256, EdDSA, PS256}, symmetric alg, `jwk` containing private members → `invalid_dpop_proof`.
- `htm` must equal the request method; `htu` compared after normalising scheme/host case and stripping query/fragment; mismatch → `invalid_dpop_proof`.
- `iat` outside [now−300 s, now+10 s] → reject (window configurable ≤ 60 s future); `jti` replay → reject.
- Tenant `dpop_nonce=required`: missing/stale nonce → 400 `use_dpop_nonce` + fresh `DPoP-Nonce`; nonces are HMAC-derived, valid 5 min, no storage.
- `dpop_jkt` accepted in PAR and stored on the code; token request proof key must match (E08_02).

- Fuzz target `dpop_proof`; FAPI2 conformance DPoP tests pass; test vectors from RFC 9449 §4.2 reproduced.

title: CSPRNG token generation & secret-handling utilities (constant-time compare, zeroize)
description:
`OpaqueToken::generate(bits)` (default 256) base64url without padding; `Secret<T>` with `zeroize`; `ct_eq` wrapper (subtle) used for every secret comparison; hashing helper `sha256_hex` for at-rest storage.

Spec: FAPI 2.0 SP §5.4.1 item 4 (credentials not handled by end users ≥128 bits of entropy); RFC 6749 §10.10 (credential guessing); RFC 8628 §6.1 (user-code entropy — used later).

Depends on: E01_01

Definition of done (project rule): spec-derived or conformance-suite test passes; fuzz target exists for every new parser/validator; threat-model note updated; no new `unsafe`; generated crypto/parsing code is not done until a human has read the cited spec sections.
acceptance_criteria:
- Statistical sanity test on generator output (no repeats in 10^6 draws, byte distribution).
- A custom lint/grep test fails the build if `==` is used on `Secret`/`OpaqueToken` types.
- All comparisons of codes, tokens, PKCE verifiers, CSRF tokens go through `ct_eq` (reviewed checklist in PR template).
close_reason: OpaqueToken::generate defaults to 256 bits, base64url unpadded; generate_bits::<BITS>() makes the 128-bit FAPI 2.0 SP s5.4.1 floor a compile error via a const assert rather than a Result. Secret<T> and OpaqueToken deliberately do not implement PartialEq, so == on them does not compile; secret_audit.rs asks the compiler whether the trait is still absent (inherent-vs-trait associated const) so a future #[derive(PartialEq)] fails the build, and greps for the one remaining exit, secret.expose() == candidate, folding continuation lines so rustfmt cannot split a comparison into two innocent halves. I verified BOTH mechanisms myself by injecting violations: the derive produces two independent errors, and the grep half located the injected expose() comparison by file and line. ct_eq via subtle for every secret comparison; sha256_hex for at-rest lookup. Statistical test is a collision check plus Pearson chi-square over the 64-symbol alphabet, counting only the 42 fully-determined 6-bit groups (the 43rd character carries 4 bits and would make a correct generator look skewed), ~1ms. No fuzz target: from_presented validates nothing by design, so no attacker-controlled bytes become a typed value. Implemented by a subagent in a worktree; merged with conflicts in Cargo.toml, domain lib.rs and the threat model resolved by hand.

title: Key lifecycle & automated rotation (encrypted at rest, KMS port)
description:
States `pending → active → retiring → retired`. Per-tenant rotation schedule; private keys encrypted with a KEK obtained from a `Kek` port (local file / env for dev, cloud KMS adapters later). Separate keys per purpose (id_token/access_token signing, SET signing may share; encryption keys separate).

Spec: OIDC Core §10.1.1 (rotation of asymmetric signing keys: publish new key, then sign with it; keep old for verification); FAPI 2.0 SP §6.8 (key compromise: automated regular rotation, single-purpose keys).

Depends on: E02_01

Definition of done (project rule): spec-derived or conformance-suite test passes; fuzz target exists for every new parser/validator; threat-model note updated; no new `unsafe`; generated crypto/parsing code is not done until a human has read the cited spec sections.
acceptance_criteria:
- Rotation test: tokens signed before rotation still verify via JWKS until grace end; new tokens use the new `kid`; retired keys are not published.
- Private key material at rest is ciphertext (test reads DB row and asserts it does not parse as JWK).
- Admin API endpoint triggers rotation; audit event emitted; concurrent rotations serialised with a DB lock.
- Same key is never used for both signing and encryption (enforced by `purpose` column + test).
notes: From ast-mxc.2: the JWKS endpoint currently uses a fixed Cache-Control max-age of 300s (crates/server/src/http/protocol.rs, JWKS_MAX_AGE). The acceptance for mxc.2 wants max-age = rotation-interval/4, which needs the rotation schedule this ticket owns. Wire it when the schedule exists, and make sure the cache lifetime stays shorter than the retiring grace period - a verifier must refetch before the key it holds stops being published.
close_reason: States pending/active/retiring/retired with a per-tenant schedule; private keys sealed with AES-GCM under a KEK from a Kek port (LocalKek for dev, async so a cloud KMS fits). Implemented by a subagent in a worktree. Verified independently: I read the stored bytes out of PostgreSQL and they are opaque (73d66d26..., not a DER SEQUENCE), nonce is 96 bits, length is PKCS#8 + 16-byte GCM tag, kek_id is derived, and a rotation leaves active+pending which is publish-before-sign. Notable: RandomizedNonceKey means the code physically cannot supply a nonce twice, backed by a unique index on (kek_id, nonce); AAD binds tenant/kid/purpose/alg length-prefixed so a moved or relabelled row is undecryptable; schedule periods are bigint seconds not interval, because a month has no fixed length and a grace period must not differ in February. The agent's first concurrency test passed without the lock, so it demoted it to an idempotence test and wrote one that actually fails when the lock is removed. Spec correction accepted and verified against the Final text: key compromise is FAPI 2.0 SP s6.8, not s6.7 (s6.7 is Client Impersonating Resource Owner) - I corrected 2 citations in crates/domain/src/audit and 5 in docs/BACKLOG.md. 381 tests. Runtime wiring is a separate ticket (filed): the binary still uses LocalKeyStore.

title: JWT verification service (typ, crit, skew window, duplicate-kid selection)
description:

Spec: RFC 8725 §3.1–3.3 (alg verification, key/alg binding), §3.5 (crit), §3.8–3.9 (validate all claims, use UTC), §3.11 (explicit typ); FAPI 2.0 SP §5.3.2.1 item 13 ('shall accept JWTs with an iat or nbf timestamp between 0 and 10 seconds in the future but shall reject JWTs with an iat or nbf timestamp greater than 60 seconds in the future'); §5.4.3 (duplicate kid selection algorithm).

Depends on: E02_01

Definition of done (project rule): spec-derived or conformance-suite test passes; fuzz target exists for every new parser/validator; threat-model note updated; no new `unsafe`; generated crypto/parsing code is not done until a human has read the cited spec sections.
acceptance_criteria:
- Missing or mismatching `typ` rejected when the context requires one (`dpop+jwt`, `oauth-authz-req+jwt`, `at+jwt`, `logout+jwt`, `secevent+jwt`).
- Unknown `crit` parameter → reject; `alg` outside caller's allow-list → reject; key type/alg mismatch → reject (RS/HS confusion test).
- Clock skew: iat/nbf up to +10 s accepted; +11..+60 s accepted only if tenant config raises the window (max 60); +61 s rejected; expired `exp` rejected with 0 s leeway by default.
- Duplicate-kid test set: verifier iterates candidate keys matching `kid` and selects by `alg`/`kty`/`crv`/`use` per FAPI 2.0 SP §5.4.3.
- Maximum JWT size 8 KiB (configurable); fuzz target on claims parsing.
close_reason: One verifier for every JWT the server accepts (client assertions, DPoP proofs, request objects, id_token_hint, CIBA, logout tokens). Policy has no Default - typ and the algorithm list are decisions a caller must make. Checks ordered so cost precedes trust: size before parsing, structure and crit, algorithm against the caller's list, signature against a resolver-chosen key, claims last. FAPI 2.0 SP s5.3.2.1 item 13 implemented exactly: iat/nbf 0-10s ahead accepted, >60s refused, and with_future_skew clamps rather than rejects so a misconfiguration yields a compliant server. exp has zero leeway; a string NumericDate is not a NumericDate. aud checked in both RFC 7519 s4.1.3 spellings. s5.4.3 duplicate-kid handling: candidates filtered by algorithm then each tried, with a test that puts the decoy first so passing cannot be an ordering accident. 8 KiB default size cap, configurable. jws::Header.kid became Optional because a DPoP proof carries jwk instead (RFC 9449 s4.2). 48 jose tests; jwt_verify fuzz target added, coverage gate at 8 parsers.

title: Multi-tenancy & issuer resolution middleware
description:
Tenant = issuer. Issuer shape `https://{host}/t/{tenant}` (path-based) with optional custom host per tenant. Middleware resolves the tenant from host/path before any protocol handler runs; all protocol routes are tenant-scoped; all keys, clients, users, sessions are tenant-partitioned.

Spec: RFC 8414 §3.1 (path-insertion well-known form for issuers with a path); OIDC Discovery §4 (path-appending form); MCP Authorization 2025-11-25 'Authorization Server Metadata Discovery' (clients try both forms).

Depends on: E01_03

Definition of done (project rule): spec-derived or conformance-suite test passes; fuzz target exists for every new parser/validator; threat-model note updated; no new `unsafe`; generated crypto/parsing code is not done until a human has read the cited spec sections.
acceptance_criteria:
- Two seeded tenants have distinct issuers, JWKS and clients; a client of tenant A cannot authenticate at tenant B's endpoints (`invalid_client`).
- Both `/.well-known/openid-configuration/t/{tenant}` and `/t/{tenant}/.well-known/openid-configuration` resolve (ties into E04_01).
- Tenant lookups are cached in-process with invalidation on admin change; no Redis.
close_reason: Tenant = issuer, resolved before any handler runs. asterius_oidc::tenancy::route is pure and accepts both well-known forms (OIDC Discovery s4 path-appending and RFC 8414 s3.1 path-insertion), rejecting a path-insertion suffix that is not exactly a tenant. TenantId::parse admits only [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,63} — no dot, no percent, no upper case — so traversal and encoding tricks are refused before the directory is consulted; config validates tenant ids too. The middleware verifies the host belongs to the resolved tenant (issuer authority or custom_host), so a tenant cannot be reached through a host it does not own; absent/disabled/wrong-host all return an identical 404. It rewrites the path, so handlers mount at /authorize and never see tenancy — applied via Router::fallback_service because Router::layer runs after routing. Behind a proxy, X-Forwarded-Host/Forwarded host is believed only from trusted CIDRs. TenantDirectory caches an immutable snapshot with explicit invalidate() plus a 30s TTL for other replicas; no Redis. Binary bootstraps configured tenants idempotently at startup. 143 tests, 1.9s. Deferred: the invalid_client half of the acceptance needs a client model — noted on ast-m9c.2.

close_reason: Audit core: AuditEvent with actor + delegation chain (RFC 8693 act), subject/client/session/grant links (FAPI 2.0 SP s6.7 item 4), closed EventType vocabulary, AuditSink port. title: Nothing promotes a pending signing key except a process restart
description:
ast-a05.14 built CachedSigner on the premise, stated in its own module documentation, that 'a key promoted from pending to active by the background sweep must reach the signer'. There is no background sweep. The only caller of TenantKeyStore::apply_schedule in the binary is main.rs:112, at boot, once per tenant.

Consequences:
- A key staged as pending is never promoted to active while the process runs. Rotation happens only when somebody restarts the server, which is not a rotation policy.
- A key whose grace has expired is never retired, so it stays in the published JWKS indefinitely.
- A tenant created after boot (admin API) gets no signing keys at all until the next restart, so every token request for it fails with NoSigningKey.

CachedSigner's 60-second TTL is the right half of this: once something promotes a key, the signer picks it up within a minute, on any replica. What is missing is the something.

Wants a periodic task in the composition root that walks the tenant directory and calls TenantKeyStore::apply_schedule, plus tenant creation calling it directly so a new tenant is usable immediately. Multiple replicas running it concurrently is safe (apply_schedule is transactional and idempotent) but wasteful; decide whether to leave it or take an advisory lock.
acceptance_criteria: A key staged as pending becomes active, and a key past its grace becomes retired, in a long-running process with no restart. A tenant created through the admin API can sign a token without a restart. A test drives a promotion through the running task rather than by calling apply_schedule by hand.
notes: Discovered while closing ast-a05.14. The signer's staleness bound is 60s (CachedSigner::DEFAULT_TTL); the sweep interval should be well under the shortest propagation period the schema permits (1 second) is impossible, so the real constraint is that promotion latency = sweep interval + TTL, which must stay far below the grace period.

title: Token endpoint must map DomainError::NoSigningKey to an HTTP response
description:
ast-a05.12 made the signer refuse rather than substitute a key when the tenant holds none of the algorithm a client registered. Nothing renders that refusal yet, because no grant handler exists.

The client did nothing wrong, so the choice of error is a disclosure decision, not a mechanical one. RFC 6749 §5.2 defines no code for 'this server is misconfigured' — server_error and temporarily_unavailable are §4.1.2.1 authorization-endpoint codes. crates/server/src/http/token.rs already answers an unimplemented-but-advertised grant with 501 and temporarily_unavailable, on the reasoning that the client did nothing wrong; the same reasoning may apply here, or a 500 may be more honest since retrying will not help.

Whatever is chosen: log it at error level with the tenant, the client and the algorithm, because it is an operator's fault and nothing else in the system will report it. Do not echo the algorithm to the client — actually the client sent it, so it is not a disclosure, but the description must still be a constant per §5.2 practice in that file.
acceptance_criteria: A token request from a client whose registered id_token_signed_response_alg the tenant has no active key for produces a documented HTTP status and OAuth error code, an error-level log naming tenant/client/algorithm, and no token. A test names the behaviour.

title: Registration accepts an id_token_signed_response_alg the tenant has no key for
description:
A client may register id_token_signed_response_alg: ES256 against a tenant whose only active signing key is EdDSA. Registration succeeds; the failure surfaces later, at the first token request, as DomainError::NoSigningKey — after the fix for ast-a05.12 the request is refused rather than mis-signed, which is correct but late. The client is told nothing at the moment it could act on it (RFC 7591 §3.2.2 has an error response for exactly this kind of unacceptable metadata value).

Two places could hold the check and they are not equivalent:

- At registration (crates/server/src/http/register.rs + ClientMetadata::validate): refuse the document. Needs the validator to know which algorithms the tenant holds active keys for, which ClientMetadata::validate currently has no access to — it takes Capabilities, not a key set. Also races: a key can be retired after a client registers.
- At tenant provisioning: stage an active key for every algorithm in SigningAlgorithm::ALL, so the question cannot arise. TenantKeyStore::apply_schedule currently stages only SigningAlgorithm::DEFAULT. Three keys per tenant instead of one, and an unused RSA key per tenant is not free.

Probably both: provision all three by default, and refuse a registration naming an algorithm the tenant genuinely lacks.
acceptance_criteria: A registration naming an id_token_signed_response_alg the tenant holds no active key for is refused at registration with an RFC 7591 §3.2.2 error, or the tenant is provisioned so that every permitted algorithm has an active key. Either way a client cannot reach a token request that fails with NoSigningKey.

title: Wire DpopEndpoint into the token and PAR handlers
description:
ast-a05.6 built asterius_server::http::dpop::DpopEndpoint and left it unmounted: crates/server/src/http/protocol.rs was owned by another agent that round, and both TokenContext and PushContext are built with struct literals there, so adding a field would have broken the build in the worktree.

Wiring needed, all of it additive:

1. ClientEndpoints gains `dpop: Arc<DpopEndpoint>`, built with `DpopEndpoint::for_capabilities(replay, &capabilities, secret)` — the constructor already makes the 'nonces iff Feature::DpopNonce' decision.
2. token_endpoint: call `dpop.check(&tenant, Endpoint::Token, &Method::POST, &headers, now).await` BEFORE token::token(...); on Err return `refusal.into_response()`. On Ok(Some(binding)) keep the jkt for the grant handler and call `DpopEndpoint::supply_nonce(&mut response, &binding)` on the way out (RFC 9449 s8.2). On Ok(None), `DpopEndpoint::required_for(&client)` decides whether to answer `Refusal::missing_proof()` (RFC 9449 s5.2) — that check has to run after client authentication, so it belongs inside or just after token::token.
3. pushed_authorization_request: same check with Endpoint::PushedAuthorizationRequest, then `dpop::reconcile_par_key(binding.as_ref().map(|b| &b.jkt), request.dpop_jkt.as_deref())` and store the result in PushedRequest.dpop_jkt (RFC 9449 s10.1 requires both spellings to be supported).
4. The authorization_code grant (ast-a05.2) calls `dpop::check_pinned_key(stored.dpop_jkt.as_deref(), binding.as_ref().map(|b| &b.jkt))` (RFC 9449 s10, FAPI 2.0 SP s5.3.2.1 item 12) and puts `proof.confirmation()` in the token's cnf.

Everything above is already built and unit-tested in crates/server/src/http/dpop.rs and crates/server/tests/dpop.rs; this bead is the mounting only.
acceptance_criteria: A token request with a valid DPoP proof reaches the grant handler with a jkt; one with two DPoP headers, a wrong htu/htm, a replayed jti or (with the flag on) no nonce gets the RFC 6749 s5.2 error object DpopEndpoint already renders; the PAR endpoint accepts both s10.1 spellings and refuses a disagreement.

title: Carry claims_locales and the parsed claims request onto the grant
description:
ast-1sk.4 built `asterius_oidc::claims::resolve`, which takes (user, granted scopes, granted claims request, claims_locales). Two of those four have no wire yet.

**`claims_locales` (OIDC Core §5.2).** `ClaimsLocales::parse` exists and is unit-tested, but `authorize::validate` does not read the parameter: that round was restricted to the `claims` parameter alone, because another story was editing authorize.rs nearby. One line to parse it, one field on `AuthorizationRequest`, and it has to reach the grant — a locale preference belongs to the authorization it was expressed in, not to whichever token request happens to arrive later.

**The `claims` request itself.** `AuthorizationRequest.claims` is parsed and validated at push time, and `grants.claims` is a jsonb column the model already validates as an object. Nothing copies one to the other, so `resolve` currently has no consented claims request to be given. The copy is the consent boundary: what is stored is what the user agreed to, and `resolve`'s contract is that it is handed the grant's copy and never the request's.

Note the shape question this raises: `Grant.claims` is `serde_json::Value`, and `ClaimsRequest` is the parsed form. Either the grant stores the raw object and the token endpoint re-parses it (a second parse of a value that was already checked), or the grant stores a canonical serialisation of the parsed request. The `claims_request` fuzz target already asserts that an accepted request survives a round trip through the second shape.
acceptance_criteria: claims_locales is parsed at PAR and stored; the parsed claims request reaches the grant; claims::resolve is called with the grant's copy at ID token issuance and at UserInfo; a test shows a claims request narrowed at consent does not widen at issuance

title: grants needs a claimed_at column (grant lifecycle cannot be expressed without it)
description:
`ast-uwv.2` was implemented against the baseline `grants` table as it stands, which
cannot express two of the facts the grant lifecycle needs. Neither was worked
around by editing `0001_baseline.sql` (another story owns it); both are recorded
here with the shape of the fix.

## 1. No `claimed_at` — "has a credential ever been taken from this grant?"

Grant Management ID1 (`oauth-v2-grant-management-03`) §5.6 makes a grant active
"when associated tokens have been successfully claimed by the client", and says an
unclaimed grant "should be deleted by the AS after a reasonable timeout". The table
has no column recording the claim, so `PgGrantRepository` derives it:

  claimed = subject is null                 -- client_credentials: minted at the token endpoint
         or parent_grant_id is not null     -- RFC 8693 exchange: same
         or a refresh_tokens row references the grant
         or an authorization_codes row for the grant has consumed_at set

That covers every issuance path the baseline schema has tables for. The shape it
cannot see is a grant created at the *authorization* endpoint whose only credential
is a bare access token — no refresh token issued, and the authorization code row
already purged (codes live at most 60 s). Such a grant reads as unclaimed, and
`purge_unclaimed` would delete it while its access token is still live, taking with
it the only row that could have revoked that token.

Two further paths will land in this hole when they arrive: device (`ast-p2l.*`) and
CIBA (`ast-p2l.*`) create their grants at the authorization side and today have no
table of their own that references `grant_id`, so their claim evidence is whatever
refresh token or code they happen to write.

**Fix:** one column, `claimed_at timestamptz`, stamped by whatever mints the first
credential from a grant. The status derivation collapses to `revoked_at`,
`expires_at`, `claimed_at`, and `purge_unclaimed` becomes `claimed_at is null`.
Until then the deployment-side mitigation is that the unclaimed timeout must be set
longer than the longest access-token lifetime.

## 2. No record of issued access tokens

The acceptance criterion "revoking a grant inserts their access-token `jti` into the
denylist until `exp`" cannot be satisfied by enumeration: nothing records issued
access tokens (they are stateless JWTs — FAPI 2.0 SP §6.8 item 3 is the trade-off
that buys). `PgGrantRepository::revoke` therefore takes the live tokens as a
required `&[LiveAccessToken]` parameter, and what catches the ones a caller does not
know about is the grant's own `revoked_at`, resolved through the token's `grant_id`
claim at introspection (`ast-1sk.2`). Decide in `ast-a05.3` whether that is the
final answer or whether an issued-token table is wanted.

## 3. Also absent, and worked around without loss

* No `status` column and no `pending|active|revoked|expired` check constraint — the
  bead and `docs/BACKLOG.md` both describe one. `Grant::status(now)` computes it
  instead, which is strictly better for `expired`: a stored status is wrong from the
  instant `expires_at` passes until a sweep gets to it.
* No `updated_by` column, which Grant Management ID1 §6.4 lists in the query
  response. `ast-uwv.5` will need it.
acceptance_criteria: grants.claimed_at exists; PgGrantRepository derives status from revoked_at/expires_at/claimed_at only; purge_unclaimed is 'claimed_at is null'; a code-flow grant whose only credential is an access token is no longer collected
close_reason: Closed

The one acceptance criterion it could not meet is the browser one: 'Playwright run reports zero CSP violations across the no-JS and JS suites'. title: Fetch and validate sector_identifier_uri (OIDC Registration §5)
description:
A pairwise client's sector is currently taken from the registered redirect URI's host without ever confirming the client controls the sector it names. OIDC Registration §5 requires the AS to fetch the sector_identifier_uri over https and check that every registered redirect_uri appears in the returned JSON array.

Without it a client can name a sector it does not own and so be issued the *same* sub values another group's clients get for the same users — defeating pairwise subjects for both.

This is an outbound fetch of a client-supplied URL, so it goes through asterius_server::outbound and inherits ADR-0006 in full: address-level SSRF checks, no redirects followed, negative caching, rate limiting. Do not add a second fetch path.
acceptance_criteria: sector_identifier_uri is fetched through the ADR-0006 outbound path; registration fails when the document omits any registered redirect_uri, is not an https URL, or cannot be fetched; the sector used for derivation is the sector_identifier_uri host, not the redirect host; SSRF cases covered by the existing outbound tests.
notes: Reported by the ast-2vk.6 agent. crates/domain/src/entities/client.rs already defers this. Depends on ast-mxc.5 (done).

title: Wire PgKeyRepository into the server (keys are still in-memory at runtime)
description:
ast-mxc.3 built PgKeyRepository with encryption at rest, rotation states and a KEK port, and it implements the domain KeyStore port. The binary still constructs asterius_jose::LocalKeyStore, so at runtime every tenant's signing key is generated at startup and lost on restart: tokens signed before a restart stop verifying, the JWKS changes on every boot, and none of the encryption-at-rest or rotation work is reachable.

Two shape mismatches to resolve: PgKeyRepository::new(pool, tenant, kek, audit) is per-tenant, while ProtocolState holds a single Arc<dyn KeyStore> whose methods already take a TenantId; and the KEK has to come from configuration (a Kek port implementation chosen at boot, LocalKek for dev).

Also add TenantScope::keys() so the crate's 'every repository hangs off TenantScope' documentation stays true.
acceptance_criteria: Server signs and serves JWKS from PostgreSQL; a restart preserves kids and previously signed tokens still verify; the KEK source is configurable and its absence is a startup error, not a silent fallback; TenantScope::keys() exists.
close_reason: TenantKeyStore adapts the tenant-scoped PgKeyRepository to the multi-tenant KeyStore port the router holds, building a repository per call rather than making the repository tenant-agnostic - that would delete the cross-tenant check, which is worth more than an allocation. It lives in store-pg, not server, because it holds a PgPool and the server crate deliberately has no sqlx dependency. KEK source is [keys] kek_file or kek_env, exactly one, no default: a generated-on-boot KEK could not open yesterday's rows and the failure would look like corruption. Startup runs apply_schedule (which creates the first key for a new tenant and applies the schedule for an existing one - same call, so bootstrap cannot diverge from steady state) and then decrypts the active key, so a wrong KEK fails the boot naming both key ids instead of failing the first token. No grant handler issues one yet (ast-a05.*), so there is nothing to deny today; this lands with issuance.

title: Revoke a registration access token presented at the wrong client
description: RFC 7592 §2.1/§2.2/§2.3: a registration access token presented for a client that does not exist SHOULD be immediately revoked. ast-m9c.5 deliberately does not, because honouring it needs a lookup by digest across the tenant's clients on a request that has not authenticated, and 'clients' has no index on registration_access_token_hash — a sequential scan per hostile request at an endpoint that is not yet behind ast-p2l.3. Needs: a migration adding a partial index on (tenant_id, registration_access_token_hash) where not null, and a tenant-scoped 'update clients set registration_access_token_hash = null where tenant_id = $1 and registration_access_token_hash = $2' on the refusal path. Weigh it against the lockout: this server issues no client secret, so the registration access token is a client's only credential and has no re-issue path (RFC 7592 §5 warns about exactly that state).
acceptance_criteria: A token presented at a client_id it does not own is revoked and its own client's next request is a 401; the revocation is a single indexed statement, never a scan; a request presenting a token no client holds writes nothing; the refusal is byte-identical either way, so revocation is not observable.

title: Per-tenant registration policy, and stop advertising a closed registration_endpoint
description:
ast-m9c.4 landed the registration gate as a deployment-wide setting: [registration] mode = "closed" | "initial_access_token" | "open" in asterius.toml, read into crate::http::register::RegistrationPolicy. Two gaps follow.

1. The bead describes a per-tenant choice ("tenant may enable open registration only together with a DCR policy"), and per-tenant flags do not exist yet — the discovery handler carries the same note against ast-f7m.4. Today every tenant on a process shares one posture, so opening registration for one tenant opens it for all.

2. Endpoint::Registration has no required_feature, so a deployment with mode = "closed" still advertises registration_endpoint in its discovery document and answers 403 there. 403 is the right answer for the endpoint as mounted (the URL is correct, the caller is not), but a closed deployment arguably should not list the endpoint at all. Gating the advertisement means a capability flag, and because the policy is per tenant it means a per-tenant one — which is why this is one bead rather than two.

Note the ordering constraint: whatever gates the advertisement must gate the route too, or the "advertised iff mounted" parity test in ast-o0t.3 breaks.
acceptance_criteria: Registration policy is resolved per tenant rather than per process; a tenant with registration closed does not advertise registration_endpoint; the advertised-iff-mounted parity test still passes; changing one tenant policy does not change another.

title: Audit redaction classifies OAuth error codes as credentials
description:
asterius_domain::audit::redaction::classify treats any run of >=22 base64url characters using >=12 distinct ones as an opaque credential. Several OAuth error codes match: temporarily_unavailable is 23 characters over 15 distinct, so Detail::text("reason", "temporarily_unavailable") stores [REDACTED:credential:<fp>] instead of the code.

That contradicts redact() own documentation, which promises "ordinary text is returned unchanged, so a client name, an error code or a scope list survives". invalid_client_metadata (23 chars, 11 distinct) survives only by one character.

Worked around in ast-m9c.4 by adding Detail::label(key, &'static str), which skips the scanner for values that are compile-time constants and therefore cannot have come from a request. That is the right escape hatch, but it is opt-in: any existing or future Detail::text call with an error code still loses it.

Options: (a) audit every Detail::text call site and move the closed-vocabulary ones to Detail::label; (b) teach classify about the registered OAuth/OIDC error-code vocabulary; (c) require a minimum ratio of non-underscore distinct characters, since a snake_case identifier is not shaped like a base64url draw. (a) is the cheapest and does not weaken the scanner.
acceptance_criteria: No Detail::text call site in the workspace passes a value from a closed server-owned vocabulary; a test asserts that every EventType and every OAuth error code this server emits survives redaction unchanged.
close_reason: Merged and mounted; full gate green. The redaction fix corrects the classifier itself rather than routing around it, so every Detail::text call site is covered.

title: Configuration key for the shared DPoP nonce secret
description:
asterius_jose::dpop::NonceIssuer derives every DPoP nonce from an HMAC key. DpopEndpoint::for_capabilities takes that key as an Option<&[u8]> and generates a per-process one when it is None.

Per-process is correct for one replica and wrong for several: two replicas would reject each other's nonces and every restart would invalidate the outstanding ones. Neither is a security problem — the client is told use_dpop_nonce and retries with the value it is handed, which RFC 9449 s8 calls self-correcting — but it turns the retry from a once-per-client event into a per-request coin flip, which is exactly the behaviour the one-window lookback exists to avoid.

Needed: a config key (something like [dpop] nonce_secret, alongside the KEK's spelling in crates/server/src/config.rs — env var, file, or base64 literal, with the same refusal-to-start behaviour when it is malformed), passed to DpopEndpoint::for_capabilities. Only meaningful when Feature::DpopNonce is on, so it should be optional and unreferenced otherwise.
acceptance_criteria: An operator can set one secret across replicas; a deployment with the flag on and no configured secret still starts, with a log line saying nonces are per-process.

title: Advertise claims_supported, claims_parameter_supported and claims_locales_supported
description:
ast-1sk.4 landed the OIDC Core §5.4 scope-to-claim mapping and exposes `asterius_oidc::claims::claims_from_scopes()`, which generates the §5.4 half of Discovery §3's `claims_supported` from the table rather than from a hand-written list. Nothing publishes it yet: `crates/oidc/src/metadata.rs` was owned by another story that round and was left alone.

Wire up, in metadata.rs:

* `claims_supported` — `claims_from_scopes()` plus `sub` (always supplied, and in no scope's list) plus whatever a tenant's own claims add. Deciding whether tenant claims are advertised is part of this: Discovery §3 says the array lists claims the OP 'MAY be able to supply values for', so over-advertising is permitted and under-advertising misleads.
* `claims_parameter_supported: true` — `ClaimsRequest::parse` is wired into `authorize::validate`, so the answer is now yes and the default (`false`) is a lie.
* `claims_locales_supported` — `ClaimsLocales` resolves against whatever language tags a tenant's claim set actually carries, so this is a query over stored claim names rather than a constant. Decide whether that is worth computing or whether omitting the member (which Discovery §3 permits) is the honest answer.
acceptance_criteria: metadata advertises claims_supported generated from the mapping; claims_parameter_supported is true; a test asserts every advertised claim is one claims::resolve can produce

title: Pairwise salt is decrypted on every subject mint

With LocalKek that is a microsecond; with a KMS adapter it is a network round trip per id_token. A per-tenant in-process cache of the decrypted salt would remove it, at the cost of holding key material in memory for the life of the process and of a cache that must be invalidated when a tenant is deleted. Filed by the ast-2vk.11 agent as a deliberate deferral: the salt is written once and never changes, so the cache is trivially correct, but 'hold a secret in memory forever' deserves its own argument.

title: Subject identifiers are not tombstoned on user deletion
description:
Deleting a user cascades over subject_identifiers, which in principle frees a sub for reuse. OIDC Core §8 says a Subject Identifier is never reassigned.

In practice nothing regenerates one — the local account id is a random UUID that is never reissued — so the risk is small. But 'never in practice' is weaker than the spec's 'never', and a relying party that keyed its own records on sub has no way to tell a reused identifier from a returning user.

Needs a tombstone table that outlives the user row, and a check on the derivation path.
acceptance_criteria: A tombstone table retains deleted sub values; deriving a subject can never produce a tombstoned value; a DB test deletes a user and proves the identifier is not reissued.
notes: Reported by the ast-2vk.6 agent; the acceptance criterion asked for it but a migration was out of scope for that story.

title: Registration must refuse pairwise + loopback-only redirect URIs
description:
RFC 8252 §7.3 gives every native client the same 127.0.0.1 host. OIDC Core §8.1 derives the sector from 'the host component of the registered redirect_uri', so a pairwise client whose only redirect URI is a loopback callback would put every native client on the deployment into one sector — handing them all a correlatable identifier under a registration that says 'pairwise'.

SectorIdentifier::of_client already refuses the combination and asks for a sector_identifier_uri, but it does so at authorization time. That is the wrong moment: it should be a rejected registration document, not a request that fails later for a reason the client cannot see.
acceptance_criteria: ClientMetadata::validate rejects subject_type=pairwise with only loopback redirect URIs and no sector_identifier_uri, with the RFC 7591 §3.2.2 invalid_client_metadata error naming sector_identifier_uri; unit test covers accept/reject either side of the boundary.
notes: Reported by the ast-2vk.6 agent, which could not touch client.rs (concurrent work).

title: Make a client registration and its audit record atomic
description:
crates/server/src/http/register.rs writes the clients row, then appends client.registered to the trail, and a failed audit write does not fail the request.

That is the opposite of what TenantKeyStore::apply_schedule does for key.rotated, and the asymmetry is deliberate: a rotation refused after the fact can be retried from the key rows, but a registration refused after the row is committed strands a live client whose owner was told it failed and never received the only copy of its registration access token. So the endpoint returns 201 and logs the gap at error with the tenant and client_id.

The proper fix is the same one keys.rs names: write the audit event through the transactional outbox in the same transaction as the row (ast-0ju.9). Until then a crash or an audit-store failure in the window leaves a client with no trail entry — which for a registration endpoint reachable without a client credential is the gap most worth closing.
acceptance_criteria: A client registration and its client.registered audit record commit together or not at all; a test kills the audit path and asserts no orphaned clients row.

title: Correct the RFC 9449 section numbers in the backlog

(FAPI 2.0 SP s5.3.2.1 item 12 itself cites s10.1, which is probably where this came from; FAPI is citing the PAR subsection because FAPI mandates PAR.)
- 'RFC 9449 s10.2 (in PAR)' — there is no s10.2. PAR is s10.1.
- 'RFC 9449 s11 (dpop_signing_alg_values_supported)' — that is s5.1. s11 is Security Considerations.
- 'RFC 9449 s12 (dpop_bound_access_tokens)' — that is s5.2. s12 is IANA Considerations.
- 'RFC 9449 s13 (security: htu normalisation, replay)' — s13 is References. Security Considerations is s11; proof replay is s11.1; the htu normalisation guidance is the last paragraph of s4.3, citing RFC 3986 s6.2.2 and s6.2.3.

The code comments carrying these numbers were corrected in ast-a05.6 (crates/domain/src/entities/client.rs, crates/domain/src/entities/auth_request.rs, crates/oidc/src/authorize.rs, crates/store-pg/tests/database.rs, docs/threat-model.md). docs/BACKLOG.md line 416 and any bead descriptions still carry them.

title: client_keys table cannot express a negative cache entry
description:
The client_keys table is keyed by (tenant_id, client_id, kid). A *failed* jwks_uri fetch has no kid, so there is no row that can represent 'we tried this URI at T and it failed'. The negative cache from ast-mxc.5 is therefore in-memory and per-replica: N replicas will each hammer an unreachable third-party jwks_uri once per backoff window instead of once between them, and a restart clears the memory of the failure entirely.

Not urgent — the in-memory cache is correct, just not shared — but it becomes real when the deployment is multi-replica, which the modular monolith of ADR-0001 explicitly expects to be.

Options: (a) add a client_key_fetches table keyed by (tenant_id, client_id, jwks_uri) holding last_attempt_at / last_error / next_attempt_at; (b) leave it per-replica and document the multiplier in the operator docs; (c) treat it as covered by whatever shared cache ast-f7m picks up.

Decide before the first multi-replica deployment, not after a client complains about our traffic.
acceptance_criteria: Either a schema change lands with a migration and a DB test, or an explicit written decision to keep the cache per-replica with the traffic multiplier documented in the operator docs.
notes: Found while reviewing ast-mxc.5. The table exists in 0001_baseline.sql but is currently unused — the cache that shipped is entirely in-memory, so nothing reads or writes it yet. That is worth deciding on too: an unused table in the baseline is a claim about a design we have not committed to.
